correctness.rationale: Let X=ab+c with 1<=a<b,0<=c<b and b<=X<2X<b^2. In a no-carry doubling 2c<b, both digits double, so S3(2X)=8S3(X)=16X, contradicting required X. A carry forces c>=b/2 and a<b/2. From S3(X)=2X follows c^3<=b^2+b-2, whereas c^3>=b^3/8. The difference b^3-8b^2-8b+16 is positive at b=9 and increasing thereafter, so no b>=9. Independent enumeration of all 68 admissible digit pairs for 2<=b<=8 recovered exactly one satisfying first equation: (8,3,3,X=27), but S3,8(54)=432!=27. All bases and all two-digit cases exhausted; none beyond two digits claimed.

value.rationale: The exact ratio-two question is a mathematically motivated small-denominator dynamical rigidity test: the exponent-two map has an infinite two-digit doubling two-cycle construction, while cubic digit dynamics forbids that entire mechanism in every base. The all-base analytic cutoff plus exhaustive finite residual classification proves a genuine universal negative boundary, though it is narrow and not a census of all cubic cycles.
residual_risks: The negative result is narrow (two digits, exponent 3, factor 2); it says nothing about other ratios or larger lengths.
